items.title: Integrated Judiciary & the Supreme Court
items.body:
## A single, integrated judiciary

- India has **one integrated judicial system** (unlike the US dual system) in a **three-tier structure**: **Supreme Court → High Courts → Subordinate Courts**. The same courts enforce both Union and State laws.
- Predecessor: the **Federal Court of India** (Government of India Act, 1935). The **Supreme Court** was inaugurated on **28 January 1950**, two days after the Constitution came into force.
- Provisions: **Part V, Chapter IV, Articles 124-147**.

## Composition & appointment

- Present sanctioned strength: **34 judges** (33 + CJI); it began with **8** in 1950.
- Qualifications (Art 124): citizen of India; **5 years as a High Court judge** OR **10 years as a High Court advocate** OR a distinguished jurist. **No minimum age** is prescribed.
- Judges are appointed by the **President** through the **Collegium** (CJI + 4 senior-most judges). The **NJAC (99th Amendment)** was **struck down in 2015**.
- Tenure: retire at **65**; removal only for **proven misbehaviour or incapacity** under **Article 124(4)** via a **special majority** in each House (Judges Inquiry Act, 1968).
keyPoints: Single integrated judiciary, three-tier: Supreme Court > High Courts > Subordinate Courts.
Supreme Court inaugurated 28 January 1950; successor to the Federal Court (GoI Act 1935).
Covered by Part V, Articles 124-147; present strength 34 judges (originally 8).
SC judge qualifications: 5 years as HC judge OR 10 years as HC advocate; no minimum age.
Judges appointed by the President via the Collegium; NJAC struck down in 2015.
SC judges retire at 65; removed under Article 124(4) by special majority (Judges Inquiry Act 1968).
items.mnemonic: SC age 65, HC age 62 — 'Senior Court is older' (65 > 62).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Judiciary (Supreme Court)

items.title: Jurisdiction & Powers of the Supreme Court
items.body:
## Heads of jurisdiction

| Type | Article | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Original | 131 | Centre-State & inter-State disputes (exclusive) |
| Writ | 32 | Enforcement of Fundamental Rights; 5 writs |
| Appellate | 132/133/134 | Constitutional, civil, criminal appeals |
| Special Leave | 136 | Discretionary appeal from any court/tribunal (except military) |
| Advisory | 143 | President refers a question of law/fact (opinion not binding) |

## Other powers

- **Article 141** — law declared by the SC is **binding on all courts** in India.
- **Article 142** — the SC may pass any decree for **complete justice**.
- **Article 137** — the SC can **review** its own judgments.
- **Judicial review** — power to strike down laws/executive acts violating the Constitution; part of the **basic structure**.
- **Public Interest Litigation (PIL)** relaxed *locus standi*, widening access to justice.

## The five writs (Art 32 / 226)

- **Habeas Corpus** — produce the detained person.
- **Mandamus** — command a public authority to do its duty.
- **Prohibition** — stop a lower court exceeding jurisdiction (before the order).
- **Certiorari** — quash an order already passed.
- **Quo Warranto** — question a person's authority to hold a public office.
keyPoints: Original jurisdiction (Art 131) covers Centre-State and inter-State disputes.
Writ jurisdiction under Art 32 enforces Fundamental Rights (Ambedkar: 'heart and soul').
Article 136 = Special Leave Petition, the widest discretionary appellate power (not for military tribunals).
Article 143 = advisory jurisdiction; the opinion is not binding on the President.
Article 141 makes SC law binding on all courts; Article 142 allows orders for complete justice.
Five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto.
items.mnemonic: Writs 'HM-PCQ': Habeas, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Judiciary (Supreme Court — jurisdiction)

items.title: High Courts — Provisions & Jurisdiction
items.body:
## Constitutional scheme (Articles 214-231)

- **214** — a High Court for each State; **215** — HC is a court of record; **216** — CJ + other judges; **217** — appointment/conditions; **222** — transfer of a judge (by the President after consulting the CJI); **226** — writ power; **227** — superintendence; **231** — common HC for two or more States.
- **First High Courts (1862):** Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (under the Indian High Courts Act, 1861). India today has **25 High Courts**.
- **Seventh Amendment Act, 1956** allowed a **common High Court** for two or more States/UTs.

## Appointment, qualification, tenure

- Appointed by the **President**; for judges other than the CJ, he consults the **CJI, the Governor and the HC Chief Justice**.
- Qualification: Indian citizen with **10 years' judicial office** OR **10 years as a High Court advocate**.
- Retire at **62**; removed by the **President on a parliamentary address** for proven misbehaviour/incapacity.

## Wider writ power

- **Article 226** lets a High Court issue writs for Fundamental Rights **and for 'any other purpose'** — so its writ jurisdiction is **wider than the SC's Article 32** (which is limited to Fundamental Rights).
keyPoints: High Court Articles: 214-231; first HCs (1862) at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras.
India has 25 High Courts; Seventh Amendment 1956 allows a common HC for two+ States.
HC judges appointed by the President consulting CJI, Governor and HC Chief Justice.
HC judge qualification: 10 years' judicial office OR 10 years as an HC advocate.
HC judges retire at 62; removal by President on a parliamentary address.
Article 226 (writs 'for any other purpose') is wider than Article 32; Article 227 = superintendence.
items.mnemonic: HC writs are 'wider' — Art 226 covers FRs + 'any other purpose'; Art 32 is FR-only.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Judiciary (High Court)

items.title: High Court of Andhra Pradesh (Amaravati)
items.body:
## Creation of the AP High Court

- After the 2014 bifurcation, the **High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad** served as the **common High Court** for both Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
- A separate **High Court of Andhra Pradesh** was created by a **Presidential order effective 1 January 2019**, under the **Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014**. The common Hyderabad court continued as the **Telangana High Court**.
- **Seat: Amaravati** (Nelapadu), the state capital region — making AP one of the newest High Courts, listed alongside Telangana (Hyderabad, 2019).

## Exam-relevant points

- AP thus has its own High Court exercising **writ jurisdiction under Article 226** for the whole State.
- Below it lies the AP district judiciary; **District Judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court** (Article 233).
- Note the twin creation of **two 2019 High Courts** (AP-Amaravati and Telangana-Hyderabad) from a single common court — a frequent match-the-following point.
keyPoints: AP High Court created by Presidential order effective 1 January 2019 under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014.
Seat is Amaravati (Nelapadu), Andhra Pradesh's capital region.
It was bifurcated from the common High Court at Hyderabad, which became the Telangana High Court.
Both the AP (Amaravati) and Telangana (Hyderabad) High Courts date from 2019.
The AP High Court exercises Article 226 writ jurisdiction for the whole State.
items.source: verified — AP Reorganisation Act 2014; Wikipedia 'High Court of Andhra Pradesh'

items.title: Subordinate Courts (Articles 233-237)
items.body:
## Constitutional provisions

- **233** — Governor appoints **District Judges** in consultation with the High Court (candidate: 7 years' advocacy, not in govt service).
- **234** — recruitment of judicial officers below District Judge: Governor + **State PSC** + High Court.
- **235** — the High Court **controls** postings, promotions and leave of the district judiciary.
- **236** — 'District Judge' includes Sessions Judge, Additional Sessions Judge, Chief Judicial Magistrate.

## Hierarchy

| Side | Higher → Lower |
|---|---|
| Civil | District/Subordinate Judge → Munsiff → Small Causes |
| Criminal | Sessions Court → CJM (≤7 yrs) → JM First Class (≤3 yrs) → Second Class |

- The **same officer** is the **District Judge** (civil) and **Sessions Judge** (criminal).
- A **death sentence** by a Sessions Court needs **High Court confirmation**.

## Access-to-justice mechanisms

- **NALSA** (Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987; gives effect to **Article 39A**) provides **free legal aid** and organises **Lok Adalats**.
- **Lok Adalat** awards are **final and non-appealable**, with the status of a civil-court decree.
- **Gram Nyayalayas** (Act of 2008) are **mobile rural courts** handling civil and criminal cases.
keyPoints: Subordinate courts: Articles 233-237; District Judges appointed by the Governor with the High Court (Art 233).
Article 235 gives the High Court control over the district judiciary.
Civil hierarchy: District/Subordinate Judge > Munsiff; Criminal: Sessions Court > CJM (≤7 yrs) > JMFC (≤3 yrs).
A death sentence by a Sessions Court needs High Court confirmation.
NALSA (LSA Act 1987) gives effect to Article 39A and runs Lok Adalats.
Lok Adalat awards are final and non-appealable; Gram Nyayalayas (2008) are rural mobile courts.
items.mnemonic: Article 39A + Act 1987 = NALSA free legal aid; Lok Adalat award = final.

items.title: Judicial Independence, Review & Landmark Cases
items.body:
## Safeguards for independence

- **Security of tenure** — judges removable only for proven misbehaviour/incapacity by a hard **impeachment-like** process.
- **Fixed service conditions** — salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund; cannot be varied to a judge's disadvantage (except in a financial emergency).
- **Separation from the executive** (DPSP Art 50); ban on practice after retirement (SC judges); **contempt powers** to protect authority; conduct not discussed in the legislature.

## Judicial review & activism

- **Judicial review** — courts can invalidate laws/acts that violate the Constitution; it is part of the **basic structure**.
- **PIL** widened access; the debate on **judicial activism vs. judicial restraint** turns on how far courts should enter policy.

## Landmark cases

| Case | Contribution |
|---|---|
| Kesavananda Bharati (1973) | Basic structure doctrine |
| Golaknath (1967) | FRs held unamendable (later modified) |
| Maneka Gandhi (1978) | Expanded Article 21 (due process) |
| Vishaka (1997) | Guidelines against workplace harassment |
| S. R. Bommai (1994) | Curbed misuse of Article 356 |
keyPoints: Independence safeguards: security of tenure, protected salaries, separation from executive (Art 50), contempt powers.
Judicial review lets courts strike down unconstitutional laws; it is part of the basic structure.
PIL relaxed locus standi and expanded access to justice.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) laid down the basic structure doctrine.
Maneka Gandhi (1978) expanded Article 21; Vishaka (1997) set anti-harassment guidelines.
items.mnemonic: Basic structure = Kesavananda 1973; Art 21 expansion = Maneka 1978.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Important Constitutional Cases

items.title: Andhra Pradesh Judiciary — High Court & District Courts (2026)
items.body:
## High Court of Andhra Pradesh

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Started functioning | **1 January 2019** |
| Seat | **Amaravati (Nelapadu)** |
| Origin | Bifurcated from the common High Court at Hyderabad (Telangana HC left behind) |
| Sanctioned strength | **37 judges** |
| Chief Justice (Sep 2026) | **Justice Lisa Gill** |

## District & subordinate judiciary

- **District Judges** appointed by the **Governor** in consultation with the High Court (**Art 233**); other judicial-service posts under **Art 234**; High Court exercises **control** over subordinate courts (**Art 235**).
- Tier: **District & Sessions Court** → Senior/Junior Civil Judge courts and Chief Judicial/Judicial Magistrate courts.

## Legal aid

- **APSLSA** (AP State Legal Services Authority) under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** (Art 39A); **Patron-in-Chief = Chief Justice of the AP High Court**.
- **Lok Adalat** awards are **final and non-appealable** (status of a civil-court decree).
keyPoints: AP High Court started 1 Jan 2019 at Amaravati (Nelapadu); sanctioned strength 37 judges
Chief Justice of AP High Court as of Sep 2026: Justice Lisa Gill
AP HC was carved out of the common Hyderabad High Court; Telangana retained the Hyderabad court
District Judges appointed by the Governor with HC consultation (Art 233); HC controls subordinate courts (Art 235)
APSLSA under Legal Services Authorities Act 1987; CJ of AP HC is Patron-in-Chief; Lok Adalat awards are final

items.title: Bar Councils, Custody, Writ Scope & Article 128
items.body:
**Bar Councils / Advocates Act 1961:** the **Bar Council of India** lays down **standards of legal education**, recognises law degrees, and controls enrolment of advocates.

**Judicial vs police custody:** in **police custody** the accused is held in a police lock-up for interrogation; in **judicial custody** the accused is lodged in **jail** and the police **cannot interrogate without the magistrate's permission**.

**Writ scope:** a **Mandamus** does not lie against a **private body having no public duty**; a **Quo Warranto** may be sought by **any person**, not merely the aggrieved party.

**Article 128:** the **CJI, with the President's prior consent,** may request a **retired Supreme Court judge** to sit and act as a judge of the Supreme Court.
keyPoints: The Bar Council of India (Advocates Act 1961) sets standards of legal education and controls enrolment.
Police custody = police lock-up for interrogation; judicial custody = jail, no interrogation without magistrate's permission.
Mandamus does not lie against a private body with no public duty; Quo Warranto can be sought by any person.
Article 128 lets the CJI, with the President's consent, recall a retired Supreme Court judge.
